story_text.value:
Hey HN!

I have built SqlFlow, which is an open-source durable workflow engine backed by PostgreSQL or SQL Server, with SDKs for .NET, Java, Python, and Go. Workflows support retries, checkpoints, rate limitng, scheduling, and suspension while waiting for events.

It took a large deal of inspiration from Absurd, but it expands on the core concepts.

Instead of polling the database, it supports native database features such as PostgreSQL LISTEN / NOTIFY, SQL Server Service Broke, and you could also use NATS. The durable state always remains in your SQL database.

Each SDK comes with a complete example, that models an AI Agent Workflow:

- https://github.com/bytefish/SqlFlow/tree/main/sdks

I would love to hear your feedback.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. There are lots of API gateways out there. What we couldn't find was one with everything built-in to go from “my business logic works” to “I can safely consider publishing it on the internet”. So we spent a year building the features in APIblaze: A serverless MCP and API gateway. Here’s what makes it different:

- Authorization. Most gateways stop at authentication: they check who is calling. What they can and cannot do is left to your code or a plugin connecting to some sort of complex Authorization system. APIblaze provides users & groups management and enforces Authorization policies at the gateway, as a default suggested from your API spec. You add groups and write Authorization rules in plain English ("only whoever created a record, or an admin, can read or change that record"), tested and enforced by the gateway.

- Hosted end to end. APIblaze hosts the MCP server, the gateway, OAuth discovery and the login pages on the internet. One thing we really wanted to make easy was local development so the hosted API gateway forwards the requests to your backend, even if this backend runs on your localhost. So you can connect Claude/ChatGPT/… to the hosted MCP, bring your own oAuth and log into it (which is important because MCPs are all about taking actions and you have to know “who” is taking those actions), chat with your API to test it, and change your code live while the calls stream in your terminal.

- UI widgets: self-service API keys, users and groups and chat window. A drop-in React widget lets your users create, rotate and revoke their own keys on the developer section of your site. Another lets your customers' admins manage their own users and groups. A last one lets end users chat with your API on your App.

- Multi-tenant. Each customer gets its own keys, users, portal and MCP address to serve their own service to their end-users.

- The usual gateway tools: rate limits and quotas, transformations, custom domains and more.

- No lock-in: one command exports your setup (config, users, groups, and API keys as hashes so your callers keep theirs) to a runnable Kong bundle once you outgrow APIblaze.

To try it, paste this prompt into Claude Code or Codex, in an empty folder (you get a sample app) or in your backend's folder:

> Show me what APIblaze does using npx apiblaze skills

Or by hand, no sign-up needed:

  npx apiblaze create --target https://ninopizzas.com/openapi.yaml
It's in beta. I'd love your feedback, what you like and what you don't.

story_text.value:
If you can’t answer the question below, skip this post.

What’s the revenue tax that you are paying?

Hint: Revenue tax is a % charge levied by payments processors like Stripe, subscription services like RevenueCat, etc.

Orca is the backend monetization orchestration infrastructure we’ve built at Maxint to help us process subscriptions on any platform (iOS, Android, MacOS, Linux, Windows and Web).

Apple StoreKit was sufficient when we launched Maxint on iOS, however the launch of our Android app was constrained by Google Play Billing which required us to define the same subscription plans, entitlements and consumables, as well as to implement server side receipt validation to avoid double charges whenever a user attempts to access from a different platform than where they purchased their subscription.

We tested RevenueCat, Adapty and a dozen other subscription tools, with limited success on iOS and Android, or maybe Web. However, as we were determined to make Maxint available for any user on any platform, including desktop, we knew that we would need to build a way to handle payments across all platforms.

The result was Orca, a monetization orchestration platform supporting all major operating systems. Initially, it was rolled out with support for Flutter (Dart) only, critical for Maxint.

Today, we are announcing support for Kotlin, Swift, TypeScript (web and server) and Go (server). Available at infrastructure cost, eliminating the revenue tax exercised by RevenueCat and the rest of the subscription services.

Read the SDK docs at https://orca.maxint.com/docs/sdks

Get started at https://orca.maxint.com/ and try our MCP server at https://orca.maxint.com/docs/getting-started/ai/mcp-server/

story_text.value:
All software makes decisions. Code handles the deterministic ones. Decision models like Jev handle the judgement calls.

A decision model takes context and questions with a fixed set of choices, and returns answers with a calibrated probability. No prose, nothing to parse. Decision models are 200x faster and 400x cheaper than LLMs making comparable judgements.

I wanted to play around with decision models in more places and without writing code or manually calling APIs. I wanted scripts to read like natural language and agents to be able to pick up the tool and use it after simply reading the help output.

  brew install vsekhar/tap/decide
  decide --set-config --model typesafe:jev-latest --api-key
  API key: <paste your API key>

  decide "Is Atlanta the capital of Georgia?"
  yes

  # Choose from among options
  decide "What kind of weather is typical in Florida?" \
      --option rainy \
      --option sunny \
      --option snowy
  sunny

  # Provide context (32k context window)
  decide --context @ticket.txt \
      "Which team handles this ticket?" \
        --option shipping \
        --option billing \
        --option returns
  billing

  # Pick a level, least to most, explain each to the model
  decide --context @ticket.txt \
      "How urgent is this ticket?" \
        --level not_urgent="Customer feedback or feature request" \
        --level somewhat_urgent="Customer problem, not blocked" \
        --level urgent="Customer blocked"
  somewhat_urgent

  # Multiple questions in one call, name questions for easier parsing
  decide --context @ticket.txt \
      "Which team handles this ticket?" \
        --name team \
        --option shipping \
        --option billing \
        --option returns \
      "How urgent is this ticket?" \
        --level not_urgent \
        --level somewhat_urgent \
        --level urgent \
      "Should we issue a refund?"
  team=billing
  somewhat_urgent
  yes

  # Script-friendly exit codes
  if decide --context "$body" "Is this message spam?" -q; then
    mv "$file" spam/
  fi
Other features:

- Confidence: gate on the model's confidence in its answer with --min-confidence and --fallback

- Question files: load questions from a file, useful for detailed questionnaires under version control

- Scriptable: 0 is decided or yes, 1 is no, 2 is unsure, 10 is your mistake, 11 is network/model problem

- Agent skill: agents can get cursory information about files quickly and cheaply before or instead of reading them (example skill included in the repo) - token efficient, no MCP

- Statistics and distribution: output the model's confidence and probabilities across your choices

- JSON: read context as JSON objects, write decisions as JSON objects

- Streaming: decide once per line from stdin using --each (for JSONL pipelines)

- Economical: two orders of magnitude cheaper than LLMs (Jev: $0.042/Mtok input, free output)

- Fast: typical latency of 200ms end-to-end (400 token context with 5 questions)

- Scalable: unlimited questions per call, processed in parallel

Limitations:

- Typesafe or OpenRouter API key required

- macOS 26+ pre-built via Homebrew; macOS 15 and Linux build from source (requires Swift 6.2)

- Jev only (so far the only publicly available decision model)

See also:

- DecisionModels (https://github.com/vsekhar/DecisionModels): Swift library for static and dynamic decision model calls, inspired by Apple's FoundationModels library, and powering decide.

- llm-typesafe (https://github.com/simonw/llm-typesafe): JSON-oriented input and output, integrated into the general purpose (and very popular) llm command by simonw which is written in Python and has 14 runtime dependencies.

Swift 6.2, Apache 2.0

What do you think about the command line model? How are you plugging decision models into your systems?

story_text.value:
I've been following the Anthropic supply-chain ruling discussion here, and one thing keeps nagging at me as someone learning to build on Next.js while studying LLM app architecture: multi-model redundancy quietly stopped being an optimization and became a compliance requirement for anyone selling to the US government or large enterprises.

A single-model vendor is now officially a supply-chain risk. That makes sense at scale, but what does it actually mean for a small team? Abstracting calls behind one interface sounds easy until models diverge on tool calling, structured outputs, context windows, and latency. And who maintains the eval suite and fallback logic once you support two or three providers?

For those of you running LLM features in production: do you genuinely route across providers, or keep one hot standby? Is an abstraction layer worth it early, or does it just flatten every model to the weakest one? Curious what patterns actually hold up when vendor lock-in becomes a legal problem rather than just a cost one.

story_text.value:
I'm looking for people who are a bit more familiar with neural networks than me (I follow kaparthy's tutorial once, that's about it).

Lets say I like using LLMs for quality/complex tool-calling to e.g. solve bugs, or just be a more sophisticated researcher.

But I don't need it to write code for me. What would this look like? Would it just be a fancy NLU? Could you get a 3B tool that's targeted towards tool-calling? or maybe a 1B?

It wouldn't be more than just

```rust USER: cargo build fails with: error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `foo`

CONTEXT: foo: Vec<String>

AVAILABLE TOOLS: - read_file(path) - ripgrep(pattern) - rustc_explain(code) - run_tests(...)

ASSISTANT: <tool>rustc_explain {"code":"E0382"}</tool>

TOOL: Use of moved value...

ASSISTANT: <tool>grep {"pattern":"foo"}</tool> ```

I have a theory that scraping off the "code-writing" part would eat up a lot of time and size. I really don't care that it writes code for me, it's the best way to stay in the loop anyway, so off-loading this to a model is pretty useless for me. You could even test this against multiple tools. Maybe you could even use a frontier model to dig through earlier sessions and autoresearch better ways to improve this model.

Please let me know if something like this has been done before, and what the possibilities are today. I would love to dig deeper into this if there's a slight chance this is possible.

title.value: Ask HN: How realistic is a modern-day era NLU
